title: Managing large rabbit litters
subtitle: Keeping every kit alive when a doe has more than she can feed.
excerpt: A doe rabbit has 8 to 10 functioning teats and can comfortably raise 6 to 8 kits. Litters of 12 or more are not uncommon in productive breeds. When a litter exceeds the doe's teat count, the smallest kits get pushed off and quickly fade. There are practical steps to even the odds.
sourceNotes: Bob Bennett, Storey's Guide to Raising Rabbits (5th edn., 2009). British Rabbit Council, Husbandry Standards (2022). Merck Veterinary Manual, Rabbit Reproduction (2022).

glossaryTerms.definition: Moving kits from one doe to another to equalise litter sizes and ensure all kits have access to a teat.
The smallest and weakest kit in a litter, often born last and at higher risk of failing to compete for a teat.

content.text: The simplest check on a litter of over 8 kits is whether the doe has enough functioning teats to go around. Count the kits, count the active teats (slightly reddened and full of milk), and match them. If the litter exceeds the teat count, some kits will lose access unless you intervene.

is the most effective solution when a second doe has kindled within a day or two. Rabbits cannot count, but they can smell. Rub the kits you are moving in the hay from the receiving doe's nest box before placing them in. This covers any unfamiliar scent and reduces the chance of rejection.
Remove the receiving doe from the hutch before placing the new kits in the nest box. Give her 5 to 10 minutes away before returning. This further reduces the risk of rejection.
Aim to equalise litter sizes rather than move all extras to one doe. A doe with 7 kits is more manageable than one with 10.
Check fostered kits after 24 hours. Full, round bellies confirm they are nursing. Flat or wrinkled skin on the neck and back means they are not feeding.
Supplementary feeding when no foster doe is available

Rabbit milk is very rich; cow or goat milk alone is not adequate as a full replacement. Kitten milk replacer (e.g. Esbilac or Royal Canin Babycat Milk) is the closest match available. Warm to 38 to 39 C and feed via a 1 ml syringe, 2 to 3 ml per kit, twice per day as a supplement to nursing, not a replacement.
: the smallest kits that are being pushed off teats. Bring them up to feeding weight before leaving them to compete on their own. This is labour-intensive but saves kits that would otherwise fail.

In very large litters, rotate the kits at each nursing. Remove the three or four largest kits from the nest box for 20 to 30 minutes after nursing starts, allowing the smaller ones unimpeded access to the teats. Replace them when the doe moves away. This is a demanding regime but can save an entire litter in the first critical week.

attrs.cue: Foster doe is ignoring the new kits or thumping at the nest
attrs.cause: Kits smell unfamiliar, or the transition was done too abruptly
attrs.fix: Remove all kits, rub them thoroughly in the nest hay, and replace when the doe is out of the hutch eating. Keep her well fed and distracted.

attrs.cue: Smallest kit is cold and barely moving
attrs.cause: Hypothermia from missing multiple nursing sessions
attrs.fix: Hold the kit in your closed hands and breathe on it. Warm gradually over 10 to 15 minutes. Once it wriggles actively, syringe-feed 1 to 2 ml of warm kitten milk replacer and return to the nest.
